newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-EA-Generali pressured as bank battle hots up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EA-Generali pressured as bank battle hots up.

text.p: Investors dumped the stock of insurer EA-Generali on Thursday amid mounting signs the group it heads may lose the battle for Austria's flagship bank, Creditanstalt.

The consortium headed by Italian-controlled EA-Generali, was called to a crisis meeting on Thursday, the day after Bank Austria entered the six-year long race with a last minute bid for arch-rival Creditanstalt.

The hodgepodge of financial and industrial interests will have to raise its bid significantly if it wants to stay in the game by at least matching the 16 billion schillings ($1.47 billion) Bank Austria has reportedly offered for the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt.
Speaking to reporters, EA-Generali chief executive Dietrich Karner said the consortium would submit its final offer by Monday but declined to say whether it planned to raise its bid.

The consortium originally offered 720-730 schillings a share for about two-thirds of the government's stake. Bank Austria's bid would amount to 804 schillings schillings a share, 10 percent above their current market value.

Investors, gambling Finance Minister Viktor Klima may have no choice but to accept the financially more attractive offer from Bank Austria, sold EA-Generali's shares and hammered the stock down 8.2 percent to 3,120 schillings by the closing bell.
"It looks as though they may not be successful in their bid and there is concern that they may lose out on the (insurance) business they have through Creditanstalt," said a trader.
Shares of both Creditanstalt and Bank Austria rose more than 1.5 percent in an otherwise flat market.

International observers welcomed the news, predicting a merger of the two dominant Austrian banks, with combined assets of about 1,300 billion schillings, would shake up the country's sleepy and overcrowded banking sector.

"This planned transaction, if it occured, will undoubtedly introduce more dynamism in the Austrian banking market as a whole, which so far has lagged behind many other European banking systems in consolidation and restructuring," Moody's Investors Service said in a statement.

Moody's said it was watching Bank Austria's long-term Aaa deposit rating and the Aaa debt rating of the City of Vienna, which provides a deficiency guarantee to the bank, for a possible downgrade should the merger materialise. It added Creditanstalt's A1 rating may be upgraded in that case.
Standard & Poors also said it was monitoring the bid.

Closer to home, the reaction to Bank Austria's last-minute bid was less favourable. The Creditanstalt workers' council, sensing imminent job cuts, vowed to fight a possible union with Bank Austria and called a protest meeting for Friday.
"We want to protest against this elephant's marriage," workers' council head Helmut Wasser said.

Creditanstalt management, too, has balked at what it considers an unfriendly takeover by another state-owned firm and a political rival. The government owns 17 percent of Bank Austria, while 41 percent of its capital is effectively controlled by the City of Vienna.

Bank Austria is a stronghold of the ruling Social Democrats. Creditanstalt, which once acted as banker to the Habsburg rulers of the Austro-Hungarian empire, is a close ally of the conservative People's Party, junior partner in the coalition government.
"This is not a privatisation but under the guise of a privatisation will polarise the whole sector," said one executive, talking on condition of anonymity.

Creditanstalt and conservatives in the government have publicly backed the EA-Generali group, which includes savings bank Die Erste (First Austrian), Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana. ($1=10.86 Schilling)
